notes.meaning: Israel marched north toward the fertile region of Bashan after defeating Sihon. King Og came out to Edrei to attack them in open battle without any provocation. Og trusted in his own military might instead of learning from Sihon's defeat.

God told Moses not to fear Og's army or his size. The Lord promised that Og and his entire kingdom were already handed over to Israel, just as Sihon had been. True courage comes from trusting God's word rather than looking at the size of our challenges.

The Lord gave Israel complete victory over King Og and his army. Israel struck down every soldier, leaving no survivors behind. This decisive triumph showed that God was faithfully fighting for His people.

Israel captured all sixty fortified cities in Og's region of Argob, along with many unwalled villages. These cities had high walls, strong gates, and metal bars, yet none of them could resist God's people. This showed Israel that even the strongest fortresses cannot stand against the Lord.

Israel devoted the cities to destruction, putting all the inhabitants to death just as they had done in Sihon's kingdom. Devoting them meant setting them apart for God's total judgment, which protected Israel from being drawn into Canaanite idol worship. The people were permitted to keep the livestock and goods as plunder for themselves.

Moses describes the vast territory taken from both Amorite kings east of the Jordan River. It stretched from the Arnon Valley in the south all the way north to snow-capped Mount Hermon, covering the high plains, Gilead, and Bashan. The Lord gave Israel this entire land through their obedience and His mighty power.

King Og was the last survivor of the Rephaim, an ancient race of giant people. Moses mentions Og's huge iron bed, measuring about thirteen feet long and six feet wide, which was preserved in the Ammonite city of Rabbah. Defeating such a giant showed that no enemy is too big for God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that Og's bed was not made of metal, but was a stone coffin carved from dark volcanic basalt.

notes.meaning: Moses divided the conquered lands among the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. Reuben and Gad received the southern region up through half of Gilead, while half of Manasseh received the rest of Gilead and all of Bashan. This fulfilled their request to settle in the rich pasturelands east of the Jordan.

Jair, a leader from the tribe of Manasseh, took over the region of Argob up to the borders of Geshur and Maacah. He named those villages after himself, calling them the towns of Jair. This gave the clan of Manasseh clear ownership of that northern frontier.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many commentators hold that the phrase 'to this day' was added later by an inspired editor, like Joshua or Ezra, rather than written by Moses during the wilderness journey.

notes.meaning: Moses gave northern Gilead to the family of Machir, while Reuben and Gad received the land stretching south to the Arnon Valley and west to the Jordan River. Their western border ran along the Jordan Valley from the Sea of Galilee down to the Salt Sea at the foot of Mount Pisgah. Defining these clear borders helped prevent future disputes between neighboring tribes.

Moses reminded the eastern tribes of their promise to send their armed soldiers across the Jordan ahead of their brothers. Their wives, children, and large herds of livestock could stay safely behind in their newly assigned towns. Once God gave rest and land to the rest of Israel, these men could return home to enjoy their own inheritance.

Moses encouraged Joshua by telling him to remember what God had just done to the two kings. Joshua was not to fear any of the kingdoms in Canaan, because the Lord Himself would fight for Israel. Remembering God's past help gives believers confidence to face new challenges.

Moses pleaded with the Lord to let him enter the Promised Land. He praised God for beginning to show His unmatched greatness and power through these victories. Moses longed to cross the Jordan and see the beautiful hill country and the trees of Lebanon with his own eyes.

The Lord refused Moses' request and told him not to speak of the matter again. God held Moses accountable for his lack of faith when the people quarreled at Meribah. Even though God loved Moses, leaders carry serious responsibility and must honor God before the people.

differ.view: Moses represents God's law, which can lead people to the edge of the promise but can never bring them into the final rest.
Moses was barred because of God's earlier decree at Meribah, and his exclusion reminded the people that their own rebellion had brought this loss upon their leader.

notes.meaning: Although Moses could not cross the river, the Lord kindly told him to climb to the top of Mount Pisgah. From there, God gave him a wonderful view of the land in every direction. Even when God says no, He still cares for His servants and gives them encouragement.

God told Moses to commission, encourage, and strengthen Joshua as the next leader of the nation. Joshua was the one who would lead the people across the Jordan and help them receive their inheritance. It brings comfort to faithful leaders to know that God's work will continue through others.

differ.view: Moses represents the law, which can reveal the inheritance but can never bring God's people into it, while Joshua pictures Christ bringing believers into true rest.

notes.meaning: Israel stayed camped in the valley opposite Beth-peor, near the place where Moses would later be buried. This was where the people had earlier fallen into idolatry, serving as a reminder to remain faithful to the Lord. Here Moses paused before explaining God's laws to the new generation.
